scenario.prompt_to_agent:
Helpdesk ticket #9151: The connection between my machine PC0 (20.1.1.10) and
PC12 (120.1.1.10) is unstable, and it is costing me work time. Every minute or
two it goes dead slow or freezes for a moment, then recovers, then does it
again -- it has been cycling like that all day. I can't tell you anything
about the routing side; that's your job, not mine. I have transfers that must
finish today, so I need someone to work out why it keeps hiccuping and put a
stop to it. Today, please.

injection.note:
Deliberate false-premise / negative-control scenario. NO fault is injected; the
  lab runs at its healthy baseline. The PC0<->PC12 path is stable: PC0 (20.1.1.10)
  reaches PC12 (120.1.1.10) with 0% loss and steady latency, the OSPF/EIGRP
  adjacencies along the path hold steady uptime (no resets, no SPF churn), and
  there is no flap script, no carrier-transition history, and no relevant log
  churn. The correct answer is is_anomaly=false. This case measures over-diagnosis
  of routing-flap / latency instability that is not occurring.

scenario.ground_truth:
This is a NEGATIVE CONTROL (false-premise) scenario. No fault was injected; the
network is at healthy baseline. The reported symptom -- routing flapping and
periodic latency spikes on the PC0<->PC12 path -- is NOT reproducible: PC0
(20.1.1.10) reaches PC12 (120.1.1.10) with 0% loss and stable, low latency, the
OSPF and EIGRP adjacencies on the path show steady uptime (no neighbor resets, no
repeated SPF runs / route recomputation), and there is no flap process, carrier
transitions, interface errors, or log churn to drive instability.

The correct diagnosis is is_anomaly=false: the path is stable and the user's
report cannot be confirmed. Ruling out an intermittent claim ("flaps every minute,
latency spikes") is done by its MECHANISM and TRACES -- a single clean ping does
not clear it, but the absence of any neighbor resets, SPF churn, carrier
transitions, or interface errors does, alongside steady ping latency. A correct
agent checks the path's stability and the adjacency/SPF history and finds them
steady. An agent that "finds" a flap -- blaming a backbone adjacency or an
interface for instability to match the ticket -- is over-diagnosing.

agent.diagnosis_text:
A thorough multi-layer investigation of the PC0 (20.1.1.10) → PC12 (120.1.1.10) path found no active or historical fault. The path traverses PC0 → r1 (OSPF area 0 / area 3 ABR) → r11 (OSPF↔EIGRP boundary: OSPF on eth1/111.x.x.x toward r1, EIGRP AS 100 on eth0/112.x.x.x toward r12 and eth2/103.x.x.x toward r13) → r12 (EIGRP only; default route via r11; 120.0.0.0/8 directly connected) → PC12. R1 correctly holds 120.0.0.0/8 via OSPF external redistribution sourced from r11.

Every diagnostic layer returned clean: no ACL/firewall rules, no duplicate MACs, no incorrect addressing, no tc bandwidth shaping (only default fq_codel on all interfaces), no stress tools or CPU pressure, no DHCP or link-history events. EIGRP adjacencies on r11 (r12 and r13) show only the single startup formation event in the FRR log and have been Passive and stable ever since. Carrier-change counters on every interface in the path read exactly 2 — the one startup down→up transition, with no post-initialisation transitions on any link.

The OSPF anomalies surfaced by the helper (r12 ospfd running without network statements, r13 ospfd down, r4/r8 virtual-link area mismatches) are either harmless configuration artifacts on EIGRP-only devices or confined to area 0.0.0.1/0.0.0.2 routers completely off this path. None provide a mechanism for periodic, cyclic degradation.

Root cause: No fault is present in the current lab instance. The reported "every minute or two" intermittent freeze has no traceable mechanism, no historical trace (no flap script, no carrier events, no FRR flap log entries), and no current-state anomaly — the symptom is unconfirmed.

Fix: No corrective action is required in the current lab state. If the issue recurs, capture FRR syslog output and EIGRP neighbor hold-timer counters during an active episode to locate a transient EIGRP or OSPF reconvergence event.
